summary: You’ve landed on Mars. How would you reach your observation site, and how would you know where you are along the way? Journey to the Mars brings NASA imagery, terrain and science data together in one interactive map. Compare detours around a steep slope in Jezero Crater, or choose your own destination and see how each route changes your walking time and estimated energy use. Then try Mountain Tracker, our prototype that matches the skyline to the terrain to estimate your position without GPS.
details:
Background

We want to give future astronauts and rovers a mapping framework they can use on Mars and, eventually, on other planets.

This is our seventh time taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Every year, we hope to make a real contribution to space engineering. Our team includes a former member of Taiwan’s space agency, an IT engineer in the semiconductor industry, a graduate student in the performing arts, and a startup specialist at Taiwan’s Industrial Technology Research Institute.

Introduction

When we first read the challenge, we felt that existing tools could already bring datasets together as map layers, just as the challenge description suggested. We wanted to take that a step further.

Think more

We downloaded the maps, put them together, and asked ourselves a question. Suppose one of our teammates were landing on Mars next week (never mind the months it would take to get there). What would they want to know? Weather, temperature, radiation. It sounded a lot like getting ready for a trip. Apart from the weather, we found data for the layers we wanted. The resolution is often coarse, with a single cell covering a large area. We figured Martian weather might be a little easier to deal with than Earth’s, though Mars certainly has its share of fierce storms. We added terrain and geological resource maps to the mix as well.

Maps and layers

In our Jezero science mission, the guide suggests thermal inertia and olivine abundance as layers to inspect. In Free Exploration, you choose the layers yourself. A warning appears in the map’s information panel when a historical temperature or radiation reading in the selected area exceeds a threshold you set. Temperature comes from reports at Jezero and Gale, and radiation from Curiosity’s detector at Gale.

Google Maps inspired our route planner. On Mars, a detour around a steep slope might also save energy. Our planner estimates relative energy use from the terrain, and you can adjust the slope and surface assumptions. It generates three alternatives for the same endpoints. You can choose the shortest, the lower-risk or the lowest-estimated-energy route. You can compare their estimated walking times. In the future, we would like to model an astronaut’s oxygen supply, battery capacity and solar charging.

Navigation!

Now imagine our teammate has made it to Mars and is setting out on that adventure. We want them to be able to complete the mission with our map. First, though, they have to find themselves on it. The GPS satellites orbiting Earth are a long way from Mars, and we cannot count on a comparable network there. That leaves our map and the equipment the astronaut or rover carries.

Two things inspired our Mountain Tracker: playing The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild on Nintendo Switch, and learning how star trackers work aboard satellites. Our goal is to photograph distinctive features on mountains, or even the entire skyline, and use them to work out where the observer is standing. We found precedents in research on aerial imagery from drones and in recent work by researchers at JPL.

We took the positioning system as far as we could. We hope to pair it with gyroscopes and optical instruments carried by astronauts or rovers, reduce the chance of getting lost, and give missions a better chance of success.

Future

Our long-term goal is for the map and positioning system to become a flagship tool for Mars exploration. With funding and a future project, we would like to use GPUs and deep learning, including neural networks, to extend this positioning workflow to worlds we have yet to explore.

Imagine having a 3D map of a planet and being able to build an optical navigation system from it. How great would that be? The demo below shows what we built in two days. We would love your feedback and a chance to keep the conversation going.

Demo walkthrough

Open the Journey to the Mars interactive map to try the mission. The project README also links to the demo, source code and data references.

Our guided mission takes place in Jezero Crater. We chose a base and an observation site so you can see how a single steep stretch changes the route.

On the opening screen, choose “Jezero Science Mission” . Find the base and observation site A on the map. Before you run the check, which part of the straight line looks hardest to cross?

Select “Check the route from the base to A,” then “Show the assessed segment on the map” to locate the steep stretch. Select “Find and compare detours” to generate the alternatives. Compare their lengths and maximum slopes. The terrain check uses slope, roughness, elevation coverage and any exclusion zones you mark.

Next, open “Layers” and select “Spectral” to see how olivine abundance varies along the route.

When we were building the map, we sometimes wondered why the reading stayed the same even after we had moved quite a distance. One cell in this dataset is more than ten kilometers across, so the base and site A can fall in the same cell. It gives us a clue about what might be worth studying in the area. An individual rock underfoot is too small to see.

In this mission the base and site A share an olivine cell. Zoom in on the steep stretch and compare what the elevation profile tells you about the route with what the spectral layer tells you about the area.

Free exploration

Choose “Switch mode” and open “Free Exploration”. Under “Mission,” select a starting point on the map, then add a destination. If you want to explore the trade-offs, adjust the terrain-risk weight or the energy assumptions before planning.

Select “Build and evaluate three routes”. With the endpoints held fixed, compare the distance, estimated walking time, slope and relative energy use for each available route.

The straight yellow line shows how far apart the two points are. Alongside it are three options: the shortest route, a lower-risk route, and the route with the lowest estimated energy use. Look at the elevation profile for the shortest route, then switch to the lower-risk route. Does it skirt a steep stretch? How much farther would you have to walk to go around it? The two routes can also overlap, depending on the locations you choose.

The comparison shows which routes meet the terrain thresholds you set. Geological units and optional thermal-inertia data can influence modeled travel costs. The other science layers provide context for choosing what to investigate.

Where am I?

To try the simulated positioning exercise in the Jezero mission, open the route elevation profile and select “Where am I on the route?” In Free Exploration, build a route first, then open the positioning exercise from the elevation profile. Pick a location along the route and submit your guess.

The orange line shows the simulated skyline at a hidden point. The dashed cyan line shows the predicted skyline at the point you picked. Once you submit your guess, you can compare it with the known simulation position(try click on the route of the map on the right).

To try a real photograph, open Curiosity’s Dingo Gap panorama. Look at the skyline, then select “Reveal NASA’s camera position.” We traced the ridgeline in this image by hand. The web page replays a result we calculated in advance. Pick the peak you would trust as a landmark before you reveal where the rover took the picture.

Try Mountain Tracker with Your Own Mars Photo

Where on Mars was your photo taken? On the mission selection screen, just below Curiosity’s Dingo Gap panorama, select “Upload your own Mars photo to find candidate locations.” Choose a photo from the region you are exploring that shows a clear boundary between the sky and the terrain. Mountain Tracker traces the skyline on your device. You can correct the outline by hand and enter the camera’s field of view and tilt. The tool then compares your skyline with the horizons predicted from the region’s digital elevation model and ranks the possible camera locations by how closely their skylines match yours.

How the map finds a route and the Mountain Tracker recognizes a skyline

Our global basemap combines the Viking optical mosaic with MOLA elevation data. For each mission area, we used Python to crop the terrain by its Martian coordinates and align it with an orthoimage of the same area. The elevation grids used on the website have a spacing of 40 meters at Jezero and Valles Marineris and 20 meters at Gale. At Jezero, we also overlay geological units so you can compare the imagery with the map and see which units a route crosses.

We built the web app with Vue, JavaScript, and Leaflet. We use A* to find paths across an elevation grid. The shortest-route option minimizes distance. The lower-risk option takes slope and surface roughness into account, and the lowest-energy option estimates how much energy each segment requires. All three must avoid the exclusion zones we mark on the map. Within a search area, the Mountain Tracker calculates the skyline an observer would see from different positions and headings. It compares each predicted shape with the ridgeline in the photograph and ranks the closest matches first.

We included four global scientific grids: thermal inertia and olivine abundance from MGS/TES, gravity anomalies from GMM-3, and iron concentration from Odyssey/GRS. We also included historical observations from two stations: atmospheric pressure from Perseverance’s MEDA and absorbed radiation dose rate from Curiosity’s RAD. The map includes 2,055 official place names and ten sample-tube deposition records from Three Forks.

Alongside the map and the route planner, we built a prototype of the positioning system we imagined. The idea is for a rover or astronaut on Mars to use the shapes of mountains to estimate their position. We also implemented a way to calculate landmark bearings that you can explore alongside the skyline data.

These studies and sources of inspiration informed our design. We did not use them to train a model for this project.

  1. Our starting point was the star tracker used on satellites.
  2. We then looked at how drone researchers estimate bearings from photographs of urban landscapes.
  3. Research on distinguishing sky from ground provided background. For this project, we used rule-based image processing. We did not train or use a deep learning model.

To try the landmark-bearing simulation, set a starting point in Free Exploration and open Mountain Tracker. Expand the section on bearings to known landmarks and run the simulated landmark solver. It uses simulated bearings to known peaks to estimate position and heading.

What we measured

On the straight line from the Jezero base to site A, one stretch reaches a slope of 27.4°, above the 15° limit we set for this simulated mission. Both detours passed the route checks. The gentler of the two adds about 680 meters of walking and brings the maximum slope down from 8.8° to 5.4°.

We tested positioning with three panoramas taken by Curiosity. When we included terrain up to 90 kilometers away, the top-ranked location for Dingo Gap was 815 meters from NASA’s recorded camera position. The other two estimates were off by about 1.45 and 5.70 kilometers. The mismatch between the two skylines at Dingo Gap still exceeded the threshold for automatic correction, so the display marks only a candidate position.

What we want to try next

Our code currently uses rules to find the boundary between sky and ground. Clouds can throw it off, and we sometimes have to correct the line by hand. We want to collect more Mars photographs with known camera positions and try using machine learning to identify ridgelines. We would set aside photos from different locations and keep them out of training. Then we would let the current and new methods each estimate those positions and compare their errors against the recorded locations.

If sufficiently detailed elevation maps and surface photographs with known camera positions become available for the Moon or another world, we would like to try the same method in one small area. For our first test, we would hide the camera position and see whether the shapes of the mountains in the photo would let us find it again.

AI/SI USAGE

We used generative AI to brainstorm features for Journey to the Mars, find relevant Mars datasets and navigation research, and help interpret our test results. Codex/Claude helped us write, debug, and test parts of the map and Mountain Tracker. We also used AI to draft, translate, and edit our English project description. The Mars imagery and measurements come from the mission datasets cited in our submission. Mountain Tracker estimates position by comparing the observed skyline with horizons calculated from elevation data.
